content:
Connor O'Brien: We need to tighten up backport queue triage + label conventions before we cut the first `runtime-1.20-lts` RC. Right now folks are using `backport` / `cherry-pick` / random notes in PR descriptions and it’s going to be un-auditable fast.

Connor O'Brien: Proposal labels (minimum set):
- `needs-backport` (applies to mainline PR)
- `backport-candidate` (auto-added when `needs-backport` is set + milestone exists)
- `backport-approved` (explicit approval for LTS)
- `backport-blocked` (conflict, missing deps, etc)
- `backport-risk-high` (extra gates + explicit go/no-go)
- `lts-excluded` (explicit “no” w/ reason)

Connor O'Brien: Question: do we want separate labels for “which LTS branch” (e.g., `target:runtime-1.20-lts`) vs relying on milestone?

Sahana Iyer: +1 to keeping target info as a label. Milestones get messy (esp if we end up with `1.20-lts.1` + `1.20-lts.2` in flight). Labels are easier to query in automation.

Sahana Iyer: But maybe do `target-lts:1.20` as one label, not per patch. Patch selection can live in the backport PR title.

Omar El-Sayed: For runtime we already use PR title suffixes like `[backport 1.20]` sometimes. If we standardize:
- backport PR title: `Backport <orig PR#>: <summary> (runtime-1.20-lts)`
- include `Cherry-picked-from: <sha>` lines in commit message
Then automation can find provenance.

Noah Patel: I’m worried “target label” explodes as soon as we do 1.22 etc. Still ok if we keep it only for active LTS branches.

Sofia Ivanova: Edge case: scheduler fixes often depend on tiny refactors (rename, telemetry plumbing) that we *don’t* want in LTS. We need a way to mark “needs backport but only minimal diff” or “requires manual re-implementation”. Otherwise the queue will show green but the cherry-pick will be huge.

Samir Qureshi: Could add `backport-manual` label meaning “don’t cherry-pick, rebase-minimal patch only”. Also signals to reviewers that diff won’t match upstream exactly.

Connor O'Brien: Ok, so labels update:
- `backport-manual`
- `backport-conflict` (maybe same as blocked?)
I’d rather keep `backport-blocked` as umbrella and use a reason in a bot comment.

Sean Gallagher: From SRE side: `backport-risk-high` is not specific enough. We need a clear gate:
- if `backport-risk-high`, require perf-canary run + 24h canary before promotion.
- if not, still require perf suite but can do shorter canary.
So label needs to be reliable, not “maybe”.

Connor O'Brien: Agree. Let’s define criteria in-thread so folks label consistently.

Dev Patel: From Support: can we also have something like `customer-escalation` or link to SUP ticket? We get dragged in when customers ask “is my issue in LTS” and we can’t search.

Omar El-Sayed: We can standardize a footer in PR description:
`Customer-Impact: SUP-#### (optional)`
`LTS-Eligibility: Security|Correctness|Perf-Regression|Stability|Other`
Then the bot can parse it.

Sahana Iyer: Bot can enforce template for backport PRs. For *mainline* PRs, we can’t enforce as hard, but we can at least comment when `needs-backport` is applied and ask for fields.

Marcus Lin: Please do not put embargoed CVE details in public PR templates/comments. We’ll need a separate flow for `security-embargo` where bot doesn’t echo details.

Connor O'Brien: Good call. Add label `security-embargo` that:
- blocks auto-creation of backport PRs
- routes to private checklist + restricted reviewers
- bot only comments “tracked under security process”

Noah Patel: On target selection: label on mainline PR should be `needs-backport` + `target-lts:1.20`. Then backport owner (Omar) can decide which patch release it lands in.

Sofia Ivanova: Another edge: PRs that are “fix + follow-up”. If fix gets backported but follow-up doesn’t, LTS diverges and later backports conflict. Can we label dependencies?

Sahana Iyer: We can do `backport-depends-on: #12345` but GitHub labels can’t carry values. Alternative: checklist item in bot comment:
- “Depends on:” with links
And bot marks `backport-blocked` if dependency missing `backport-approved`.

Connor O'Brien: That’s workable. We can implement as: bot posts a “Backport tracking” comment when `needs-backport` set. People reply in-thread with deps; bot edits the comment.

Samir Qureshi: Please no “reply to comment to edit” if it’s flaky. But even a static format we can manually update is fine.

Omar El-Sayed: For triage cadence, suggest:
- daily 15m queue pass (release eng + runtime backport owner)
- weekly deeper review w/ SRE for risk-high items
Queue states:
- Candidate (needs-backport)
- Approved (backport-approved)
- In progress (backport-in-flight)
- Blocked (backport-blocked)
- Done (backport-merged)

Connor O'Brien: Do we need `backport-in-flight` label? Or just assign + draft PR link?

Sahana Iyer: Label helps queries a lot. I’d add `backport-in-flight` and have automation set it when a backport PR exists.

Sean Gallagher: Also need `backport-dropped` for cases where we decide not to include in a particular patch due to risk/time, but still might be eligible later.

Connor O'Brien: Hmm. `lts-excluded` is permanent “no”, `backport-dropped` is “not this patch”. Ok.

Dev Patel: +1, we often tell customers “won’t be in .1 but likely .2”. Having a label helps us not overpromise.

Noah Patel: Criteria for `backport-risk-high`:
- touches kernel selection / scheduling decisions
- changes batching behavior
- changes memory allocator / KV cache
- modifies request routing fallbacks
- anything that previously caused incident or required rollback
We can add a short rubric.

Sofia Ivanova: Scheduling changes are almost always risk-high unless it’s a correctness fix with narrow scope + perf-neutral.

Omar El-Sayed: Suggest rubric:
- default risk = medium
- risk-high if: affects throughput/latency critical path, concurrency, memory, or changes observable behavior
- risk-low only if: docs/tests/build changes OR bugfix behind existing flag, no behavior change

Sahana Iyer: Automation idea:
1) When `needs-backport` applied on mainline PR:
- require `target-lts:*` label OR comment “no target”
- require `LTS-Eligibility` field filled
- open task list with required evidence
2) When `backport-approved` added:
- allow `rw-backport` bot to create backport PR
- auto-apply `backport-in-flight`
3) When backport PR merges into `runtime-1.20-lts`:
- bot comments on original PR with link + patch version

Connor O'Brien: Yes. Also: if original PR has `backport-risk-high`, bot should require perf-canary link before allowing merge label `lts-ready-to-promote`.

Marcus Lin: Don’t forget artifact provenance requirements: backport PR should reference original PR + Linear/Jira. Bot can enforce presence of at least one of: `ENG-####` or `SUP-####`.

Connor O'Brien: Action items:
- Connor: write 1-pager with label definitions + rubric; post in #eng-releases and link in checklist
- Sahana: prototype GitHub Action for label->comment enforcement (respect `security-embargo`)
- Omar: propose PR title + commit message convention for `rw-backport`
- Sean: confirm risk-high canary/perf requirements we’ll bake into release gates

Connor O'Brien: For now, please stop using the generic `backport` label. Use `needs-backport` + `target-lts:1.20` and tag @Omar El-Sayed for review. :thumbsup:

Sahana Iyer: I’ll also add saved GitHub searches to the release eng README so folks can find:
- “needs-backport & no target”
- “approved but no backport PR”
- “blocked > 7d”

Dev Patel: Can we include one saved search “customer escalations not yet approved”? I can have Support check it before telling customers anything.

Connor O'Brien: Yep, add `customer-escalation` label (non-embargo) and we’ll include that in the searches.

Sean Gallagher: +1. And please ensure `customer-escalation` doesn’t automatically imply risk-high. Some are tiny correctness fixes.

Omar El-Sayed: Cool. I’ll start relabeling the current queue today so we’re not migrating forever.

Connor O'Brien: Thanks all. I’ll pin the label rubric once it’s written.
